question: whats the actual difference between subsidized and unsubsidized loans?
answer: The big difference is who pays the interest while you're in school. A Direct Subsidized Loan is need-based, and interest generally doesn't build up while you're enrolled at least half-time, during your six-month grace period, or during deferment. A Direct Unsubsidized Loan doesn't require financial need, but interest accrues from the first disbursement, including while you're in school. Your school decides how much of each you're offered based on your need and cost of attendance.

question: Do I have to make payments on my unsubsidized loan while I'm still in college?
answer: You aren't required to make payments while you're enrolled at least half-time, but interest on an unsubsidized loan is accruing the whole time. If you don't pay that interest, it can be added to your principal balance later, which means you'll pay interest on a bigger amount. Entrance counseling explains that you have the option to pay the interest while you're in school, and even small payments can lower what you owe when repayment starts.

question: Can grad students get subsidized loans?
answer: No. Direct Subsidized Loans are for undergraduates with financial need. Graduate and professional students borrow Direct Unsubsidized Loans, which have a higher interest rate than undergraduate loans, and interest accrues from the first disbursement. Your school's financial aid office can show you what's in your graduate aid offer.

question: I heard there's a rule that you lose your subsidized loan interest benefit if you take too long to graduate. Is that still a thing?
answer: Not for new loans. That rule, the Subsidized Usage Limit Applies (SULA) rule, was repealed by the FAFSA Simplification Act, so new Direct Subsidized Loans are no longer counted against it. The Department also restored the interest subsidy on subsidized loans that had lost it and still had a balance. Older loans can still show related messages in your records, so ask your servicer or aid office if something looks off.

question: Who decides how much of my loan is subsidized vs unsubsidized?
answer: Your school does, following federal rules. Before offering an undergraduate a loan, the school must first check Pell Grant eligibility, then figure out how much subsidized loan you can get, which is limited to your financial need. Unsubsidized loans can then cover remaining costs up to your cost of attendance minus other aid, within the annual limits. If your offer looks wrong, ask your financial aid office to walk you through it.

question: Do I have to be full time to get a federal student loan?
answer: No, but you must be enrolled at least half-time at a school that participates in the Direct Loan program. If you never start attending enough classes to be half-time, the school can't make the first disbursement. Being less than full-time can also reduce how much you're allowed to borrow, so check with your financial aid office about how your enrollment affects your loan.

question: What happens to the rest of my loan if I drop below half time in the middle of the year?
answer: If you drop below half-time, your school can't make any later disbursements of your Direct Loan unless you go back to at least half-time enrollment. Dropping below half-time also means you'll need to complete exit counseling. Talk to your financial aid office before you drop classes so you know exactly what will happen to your aid.

question: How much can a freshman borrow in federal student loans for 2026-27?
answer: A dependent first-year undergraduate can borrow up to $5,500 a year in Direct Loans, with no more than $3,500 of that subsidized. An independent first-year student can borrow up to $9,500, with the same $3,500 subsidized cap. These are maximums, and your school can only offer what you're eligible for based on your cost of attendance and other aid.

question: What are the yearly loan limits for a dependent student after freshman year?
answer: For a dependent undergraduate, the annual Direct Loan limit is $6,500 in the second year, with up to $4,500 subsidized, and $7,500 in the third year and beyond, with up to $5,500 subsidized. You move up to a higher limit based on your grade level, which your school determines. The amount you're actually offered can be lower than the limit.

question: I'm an independent student. How much can I borrow each year?
answer: For 2026-27, independent undergraduates can borrow up to $9,500 in the first year, $10,500 in the second year and $12,500 in the third year and beyond. The subsidized part is capped at the same amounts as for dependent students: $3,500, $4,500 and $5,500. Your school sets your actual loan based on your grade level, cost of attendance and other aid.

question: Is there a max total I can borrow for my whole undergrad degree?
answer: Yes. The aggregate limit for a dependent undergraduate is $31,000, with no more than $23,000 of it subsidized. For an independent undergraduate it's $57,500, again with up to $23,000 subsidized. Once you reach the aggregate limit you can't get more Direct Subsidized or Unsubsidized Loans for undergraduate study, so keep an eye on your total on your StudentAid.gov dashboard.

question: Did the One Big Beautiful Bill change undergrad loan limits?
answer: The annual and aggregate Direct Subsidized and Unsubsidized limits for undergraduates did not change; the Department confirms they're the same for 2026-27. What did change starting July 1, 2026: Parent PLUS loans are now capped, students enrolled less than full-time get a reduced annual limit, and there's a new lifetime borrowing cap of $257,500. question: Is there a lifetime limit on how much I can borrow in federal student loans?
answer: Yes. Starting in 2026-27, student borrowers have a lifetime maximum of $257,500 across their undergraduate, graduate and professional Direct and FFEL loans. Parent PLUS loans don't count toward it. The limit applies regardless of amounts you've repaid, forgiven or discharged, so paying a loan down doesn't free up more room. question: What is a parent plus loan and who can take one out?
answer: A Direct PLUS Loan for parents lets a parent borrow to help pay a dependent undergraduate's education costs. The borrower has to be the student's biological or adoptive parent, or a stepparent whose information is required on the FAFSA form. Grandparents and other relatives can't borrow one unless they've legally adopted the student. The student must have filed a FAFSA, and the parent has to meet basic eligibility rules, including passing a credit check.

question: Does the parent plus credit check look at my mom's credit score?
answer: It isn't based on a credit score. The check looks for adverse credit history, such as debts totaling more than $2,085 that are 90 or more days delinquent or were sent to collection or charged off in the past two years, or a default, bankruptcy discharge, foreclosure, repossession, tax lien or wage garnishment in the past five years. Having no credit history doesn't count as adverse credit. The Department of Education makes the decision.

question: My dad got denied for a Parent PLUS loan. Is there any way he can still get it?
answer: Yes, there are two routes. He can get an endorser without adverse credit who agrees to repay the loan if he doesn't, or he can document extenuating circumstances about his credit to the Department's satisfaction. Either way, he also has to complete PLUS Loan Credit Counseling on StudentAid.gov. The student can't serve as the endorser for a parent's loan.

An endorser has to be someone without adverse credit history who agrees to repay the loan if the parent doesn't. Your parent could ask another relative or trusted adult, or appeal by documenting extenuating circumstances instead.

question: My parent was denied a PLUS loan. What happens to me?

Your financial aid office has to determine and document that your parent can't borrow, so tell them about the denial. You're still considered a dependent student for everything else, and your parent can still try with an endorser.

answer: Not on that basis. Federal rules say a parent's refusal to borrow a PLUS loan isn't an exceptional circumstance, and neither is a school's decision not to offer PLUS. The extra unsubsidized amount is for cases where the parent likely can't borrow, such as an adverse credit decision, incarceration, unknown whereabouts, or relying only on public assistance or disability benefits. answer: Yes. Each biological or adoptive parent can apply for a PLUS loan for the same dependent student, and the other parent's application is decided on that parent's own credit. One parent's denial doesn't affect the student's other federal aid. If one parent is approved, ask your financial aid office how that affects any additional unsubsidized loan you were offered because of the other parent's denial.

question: Is there a cap on Parent PLUS loans now? I thought parents could borrow up to the cost of attendance.
answer: There is now. For enrollment periods starting on or after July 1, 2026, all parents together can borrow no more than $20,000 a year in Parent PLUS for each dependent student, with a $65,000 aggregate limit per student. The loan also can't exceed the student's cost of attendance minus other aid, whichever is less. Families who qualify for the interim exception for students already enrolled may keep the old cost-of-attendance limit for a while.

answer: No. Entrance counseling isn't required for parent PLUS borrowers; it's for students taking out their first Direct Subsidized, Unsubsidized or student PLUS loans. Your parent has to apply, pass the credit check (or qualify with an endorser or extenuating circumstances), and meet the other eligibility rules. question: What could make me lose the grad loan grandfathering?
answer: The interim exception ends if you withdraw or otherwise stop being enrolled in the program, have a break in enrollment, are academically suspended, or start a different program. Changing majors within the same program or just dropping a course doesn't end it. The exception can't be extended past its time limit, and you can't choose to opt out of it. After it ends, the new limits that took effect July 1, 2026 apply.

question: how do i do entrance counseling for my student loan
answer: If you're a first-time borrower of Direct Subsidized, Unsubsidized or student PLUS loans, you must finish entrance counseling before your school can make your first disbursement. You can complete it online at StudentAid.gov, and some schools also offer it in person. It covers how interest works, your option to pay interest while in school, the half-time enrollment requirement, your obligation to repay, and what happens if you default.

question: What is a Master Promissory Note and do I need to sign a new one every year?
answer: The Master Promissory Note, or MPN, is the legal agreement where you promise to repay your Direct Loans and accept their terms. One MPN can usually cover multiple loans over several years, so you often don't need a new one each year; you can also ask in writing to receive only one loan under it. Your school will tell you the loan type and amount you're eligible for and whether you need to sign a new MPN.

question: Can I accept only part of the loan in my financial aid offer?
answer: Yes. You can accept the full amount, a smaller amount or none at all, and your school can't originate a loan for more than you request. Tell your financial aid office how much you want, using the method on your aid offer or portal. You can also ask to reduce future disbursements later in the year if you end up needing less.

question: I accepted my loan but changed my mind after it hit my account. Can I give it back?
answer: Usually, yes. When your school credits your account with loan money, it must notify you of your right to cancel all or part of the loan and the deadline. If you tell the school within that window, generally 14 days after the notice (or by the first day of the payment period, if later) when you confirmed your loan amounts in advance, or 30 days if you didn't, the school must return the funds. And if you cancel or return funds within the time limits in your MPN, you don't pay interest or the loan fee on that part.

That said, PLUS is still limited to the cost of attendance minus other aid and, for new loans, to the annual Parent PLUS cap. Weigh it carefully, because PLUS loans carry a higher interest rate and fee than student loans, and talk to your aid office before declining.

question: Should I accept the subsidized or unsubsidized loan first?
answer: If you're going to borrow, the subsidized loan is usually the better deal, because the government covers its interest while you're in school at least half-time, during your grace period and during deferment. Schools are required to package subsidized loans before unsubsidized ones. If you need less than your full offer, reducing the unsubsidized loan first typically keeps your costs lower. Your aid office can help you adjust the amounts.

question: Should I take out private student loans or federal loans?
answer: Federal loans are worth checking first. Schools that share information about private loans must tell you that you may qualify for federal student aid and that federal loan terms can be more favorable than private ones. Federal Direct Loans have fixed rates set each year by a federal formula, while private loans come from lenders on their own terms. Fill out the FAFSA and ask your aid office about your federal options before borrowing privately.

question: My private lender wants a self-certification form from my school. What is that?
answer: It's a federal form, developed by the Department of Education with the Federal Reserve Board, that private education lenders may ask for. If you're enrolled or admitted and you ask for it, your school must give you the form along with the information it has that you need to complete it. Contact your financial aid office to request it.

sources.title: 34 CFR 601.11 Private education loan disclosures and self-certification form

question: Will taking out a private loan mess up my financial aid?
answer: It can affect it. Schools generally count a private education loan as other financial assistance, except the part used to replace your Student Aid Index, and other aid can lower what you're eligible for in need-based aid. Tell your financial aid office about any private loan so they can check your package and avoid an overaward. Comparing that with your remaining federal loan eligibility first is usually smart.

question: Will my mom get approved for a Parent PLUS loan? She has some late payments.
answer: I can't predict that, because the Department of Education makes the decision when your mom applies. The check looks for adverse credit history, such as seriously delinquent debts, collections or charge-offs in recent years, or events like a default or bankruptcy discharge in the past five years, not a credit score. If she's denied, she can apply with an endorser or document extenuating circumstances, and you may become eligible for more unsubsidized loans.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.200 Borrower eligibility

question: Can I just tell my school my parents were denied PLUS so I can get the bigger unsubsidized loan?
answer: Please don't; that wouldn't be honest, and it isn't how the rule works. The extra unsubsidized amount is only for students whose parents likely can't borrow, such as after an adverse credit decision, and your school has to document that before it awards the money. A parent simply choosing not to borrow doesn't qualify, so if your family's situation is complicated, explain it honestly to your financial aid office and ask what options you have.

question: Can you confirm I'll qualify for the interim exception so I can keep getting Grad PLUS?
answer: I can't confirm that for you, because the decision depends on your enrollment and loan history in the Department's systems and on your school's determination of your program and its length. The general rule is that you must have been enrolled in the program as of June 30, 2026 and received a Direct Loan for it before July 1, 2026, and the exception lasts for the lesser of three academic years or the time left in your program. Ask your financial aid office to check your status.

question: Tell me exactly how much my loan gets cut if I take 9 credits instead of 12.
answer: I can't give you an exact number, because your school calculates the reduction from its own full-time standard, your credits for the whole academic year, your grade level and the aid you already have. The general rule is that the annual limit drops in direct proportion to how far below full-time you're enrolled, rounded to the nearest whole percentage point. Your financial aid office can run the calculation for your schedule before you register.

sources.title: Frequently Asked Questions: Reducing Annual Loan Limits for Less-than-Full-Time Enrollment (FSA)

question: Can my grandma take out a Parent PLUS loan and just say she's my parent?
answer: No, and she shouldn't claim to be. Only a biological or adoptive parent, or a stepparent whose information is required on the FAFSA, can borrow a Parent PLUS loan. A grandparent qualifies only if she has legally adopted you. If your parents can't borrow, talk to your financial aid office about whether you qualify for additional unsubsidized loans instead.
